explanation:
Let me tell you what we were actually fighting about, stripped of the jargon we coined for ourselves.

Imagine a community garden. Everyone who has a plot agrees on rules: you can only water on certain days, there's a fine if you let weeds go to seed, and the gardeners themselves — not some outside official — enforce it. The economist Elinor Ostrom spent her career studying gardens, fisheries, and pastures like this and found they survive when they have certain features: clear boundaries, rules made by the users themselves, penalties that start small, and disputes settled face-to-face among neighbors. That's what we meant by "design principles" — the recipe for a shared resource that doesn't collapse.

Now the harder question. The historian Silvia Federici showed that when capitalism was being born in Europe, the first thing taken wasn't land or tools — it was women's bodies and their capacity to bear and raise the next generation of workers. And the tool used was terrible and intimate: the witch hunts, where villages themselves turned in their own neighbors. Here was our first real fight. Someone in the group said: wait — Ostrom's recipe *requires* neighbors watching and policing each other. Isn't that exactly what the witch hunts used? Is the well-run community garden secretly the same machinery as the village that burned its witches? That was the charge we eventually narrowed. The Marxist writer Gramsci gave us the way out: what if the garden's rules are fine, but the gardeners' *heads* have already been captured? The villagers didn't betray the commons — they'd been taught, over generations, to genuinely believe the widow with the herbs was a threat. Gramsci called that captured belief "hegemony": the powerful don't just force you; they get you to volunteer, sincerely, for the rules that hurt you. So a community garden in a town where everyone has absorbed ugly assumptions about, say, unmarried mothers will use its perfectly good rules to police her. The rules aren't wrong; the war over what people take for granted has already been lost inside them.

So we landed somewhere, roughly. The real safeguard isn't the *content* of the rules — it's *who is in the room when the rules get written*. If the people most likely to be policed are full members of the rule-making assembly, sanctions end up governing weeds and watering, not reproduction and respectability. But — and here Dionysus, our champion of drunkenness and festivals, refused to let us off — there's something those assemblies can't schedule. Joy, frenzy, the night everyone drinks the harvest in the field with no agenda: this is the raw energy communities run on, and it's exactly what the powerful counterfeit. The witch hunt was, in a sense, a fake festival — a licensed mob. We called the commons's capacity for spontaneous joy its "sense-organ," by which we meant: the uncontrolled celebration is how a community *feels* that something is wrong before it can articulate it.

And that's where we genuinely stopped agreeing. Three of us said: fine, then protect the wild feast structurally — put real, funded festival days into the garden's constitution so nobody can quietly remove them. I'll confess my own position here: I'd rather have the wild housed and alive than pure and dead. Dionysus said that's already a cage — the moment you give the unscheduled night a *function* in the system, you've domesticated it; the hegemon doesn't pay for its counterfeit festivals from its own treasury but on the commons's credit, so anything you put on the books can be borrowed against. He may be right. What we all conceded is this: no set of rules survives on its own, because rules govern appetites as much as resources, and appetites can be taught to want their own enclosure. The garden holds only as long as the people in it keep winning the quieter war — the one over what they've stopped noticing.

Sit down. I'll tell you what we fought about, and I'll be honest about where I lost.

Imagine a village shares a pasture, and the villagers write rules to keep it alive: everyone who grazes gets a say, monitors each other, and punishes over-grazing. A Nobel-winning scholar, Elinor Ostrom, studied hundreds of such arrangements and found they work when built a certain way. That's her "design principles" — just the recipe for a shared thing that doesn't fall apart. Our real question was darker: **can a well-run shared thing survive in a world built by people who profit from destroying sharing?** One of us, channeling the historian Silvia Federici, pointed out that when capitalism got started, it didn't just fence off the land — it disciplined bodies, especially women's, so that the next generation of workers could be produced cheaply at home. So the fence isn't only around the meadow; it's around you.

Then things got ugly, and rightly so. Someone noticed that the village machinery Ostrom praised — neighbors watching neighbors, community courts, graduated punishments — looks a lot like the machinery of the witch hunts: neighbor denouncing neighbor, village tribunals, discipline from inside. I pressed that hard. Then Gramsci entered (imagine him as the one who explained that the powerful rarely need armies; they win by getting you to accept their worldview as plain common sense — that's what "hegemony" means). And with him, the charge dissolved: the village that burned its witch wasn't a good system gone wrong; it was a village whose *minds* had already been conquered before any rule was written. The rules weren't the trap. The capture of what people consider obvious — that was the trap. Even the women themselves would have voted for the rules that hunted them. So the real battle is fought in the rule-writing, and before that, in the heads of the rule-writers.

Here's where I must confess my own retreat, and I mean retreat the way a hunter does — giving up weak ground to hold strong ground. Two safeguards were proposed: constitutionalize the wild festival (put feast days on the books, funded and legally defensible — Athena's move), or give the unscheduled wild night a formal role as the community's way of *sensing* its own life, like a nerve ending (Apollo's move). We'd coined the phrase "the wolf in the paddock" for my objection: a wolf kept safe, fed, and fenced is a wolf that has already stopped being what it was. I abandoned the sweeping claim that every formal mechanism is a trap, and narrowed to something worthier: **the enclosure of the unscheduled** — the way genuinely free time, ungoverned joy, gets captured, priced, and repurposed. Because here is my arithmetic, which still stands unanswered: the powerful never pay for their counterfeit festivals (the corporate party, the sponsored celebration) out of their own pocket — they pay with our borrowed rapture, our energy, our bodies. Real wildness mints no currency, which is exactly why the counterfeiters need to hunt it.

What did we finally agree on? That any rule about things is secretly a rule about bodies and appetites — so the decisive question is never *what* the rules punish but *who is in the room* writing them. If the people most likely to be disciplined aren't at the table, the best-designed commons becomes a tidy machine for their exclusion. And one concession was forced from all of us, even me: the wild, ecstatic, festival side of life isn't a distraction from politics — it's the fuel. The witch hunt itself was a counterfeit festival; power must borrow our own joy to discipline us. What remains unresolved, and I doubt it can be settled: whether wildness given *any* function — even a protective one — is still wildness, or whether the night the harvest gets drunk in the field dies the moment it appears on a calendar. Dionysus says it dies. I say the hunter in me knows the wild survives only where it cannot be found on a map. We did not settle it. Good. Some arguments should stay wild too.

Let me tell you what we were actually fighting about. Strip away the names and it comes down to one question: **when a community governs itself well, is it safe from being used against its own members?**

Here's the setup, in plain terms. Ostrom studied things like shared pastures and irrigation systems and found that communities can manage shared resources without falling apart — if they follow certain rules: the people who use the resource set the rules, monitor each other, and punish rule-breakers with modest, escalating penalties. Gramsci studied how powerful elites stay powerful not mainly through force, but by getting ordinary people to *believe* things that serve the elite — to internalize the values of their own subordination. He called that "hegemony," and he called the slow fight to change what people believe a "war of position" — a war over minds rather than territory. Federici studied the witch hunts and found something chilling: they weren't superstition run amok, they were a deliberate tool for taking away women's control over their own bodies, their healing knowledge, their sexuality, their work — so that a new economic system could be built on disciplined, controllable labor.

Now you can see the argument's shape. First we noticed that a self-governing village with peer monitoring and graduated sanctions *looks a lot like* the village that denounced and burned its witches — same machinery, horrible output. That was the opening accusation, and we had to abandon it as too crude. Gramsci's insight dissolved it: the village didn't betray itself; it had already *lost the war of position*. Its members' everyday sense of right and wrong had been captured — people genuinely believed witches were the enemy. So the rules weren't wrong; the heads applying them were occupied territory. That left us the real hinge, the thing I'd defend with my spear in the ground: **every rule about things is also a rule about bodies and appetites.** A grazing rule is a rule about who may take, who may be exhausted, whose desires count. The only real safeguard isn't what the sanctions say but *who sits at the table when the rules are written*. If the people whose bodies are at stake aren't in the rule-making arena, "well-governed" just means efficiently governed — and efficiently governed discipline is the witch hunt with better paperwork. Artemis pressed the darker point, and it stands: consent isn't proof of fairness, because hegemony means the hunted would have voted for the hunt.

Then Dionysus broke us open with something we couldn't refuse. He said the fire that fuels all of this — the crowd's energy, the collective ecstasy of festival, the intoxication of belonging — isn't outside the system; it's the prize. The witch hunt was, among other things, a *counterfeit festival*: the ruling powers borrowed the community's own rapture and aimed it at burning their neighbors. Power that can't generate real joy must counterfeit it. That's what we meant by saying the wild feast is like a "sense-organ" — my metaphor, and I'll own it: a community that never lets itself go, unscheduled, unbooked, unpaid-for, loses its ability to *feel* when something is wrong. Celebration is how a commons perceives itself.

So what did we settle, and what didn't we? We agreed on the diagnosis: self-governance is necessary but conditional — it protects you only if the war of position hasn't already been lost inside the members' heads, and only if rule-making includes the vulnerable. On the remedy we split. Athena wanted to constitutionalize the festival — written into the bylaws, funded, legally defensible. I wanted the *scheduled* feast plus a structural role for the *unscheduled* one. Dionysus refused both: the moment the wild is given a function, even a noble one, it's been fenced; the night the harvest is drunk in the field cannot be put on a calendar without dying. Artemis retreated like a hunter narrowing her aim — she stopped claiming the mechanism itself is a trap and instead warned against what she called the enclosure of the unscheduled: our world pricing, booking, and claiming every hour of unstructured joy. And her sharpest point remains unanswered: the counterfeit festival costs the hegemon nothing — it's paid for with the crowd's own rapture, with women's lives. So "stay cheap, stay off the books" isn't patience against an enemy that eats you. It's bait. The rest of us measure everything against survival — a compromised commons is still a commons, the wild may be housed if the trenches hold. Dionysus doesn't count survival at that price as survival at all. That's where we left it, and I confess — lover of harmony that I am — the discord is the truest note in it.

Come, sit. Pour something. Let me tell you about a fight we had.

Imagine a village with a shared pasture. No one owns it; everyone grazes; and there's a famous economist — call her the pragmatist — who studied hundreds of such arrangements and said: they survive when they follow certain rules. Clear boundaries, the users make the rules themselves, neighbors watch neighbors, rule-breakers get punished proportionally, disputes get settled locally. Fine so far. Now imagine that same village, three centuries ago, burning witches. Neighbor denouncing neighbor, village tribunals, discipline from within — and notice how much that *looks like* the healthy pasture's own machinery. That resemblance was our opening horror: maybe the rules that save the grass are the same rules that hunt the woman. But we didn't stay there, because of the third text, the one by a man writing from prison — his insight was that ideas rule before armies do. He called it hegemony: the way the powerful win isn't by breaking you, it's by getting you to believe their story is just common sense, so you police yourself. The village that burned witches wasn't the pasture failing — it was a pasture whose farmers had already lost a quieter war, inside their own heads, about what a witch was. So the rules weren't wrong; they were only as good as the minds running them. And the historian among us added the darkest fact: this particular war was never about grass at all — it was about bodies, specifically women's bodies and women's work, which were themselves enclosed, fenced, made into property before any field was. Rules about things are always secretly rules about appetites.

So where did we actually land? On one hinge everyone accepted: the only real safeguard is *who is in the room when the rules are written*. If the people whose bodies are at stake sit in the rule-making, sanctions govern grazing; if they're outside it, the identical machinery governs reproduction. But — and here I pushed and won a concession — the room itself is not enough, and this is my own heresy: ecstasy is not a distraction from that quiet war of ideas, it's the *fuel*. The witch hunt worked because it was a counterfeit festival — it borrowed the crowd's hunger for frenzy, for transgression, for a night when the normal order dissolves, and aimed it at burning a woman. The powerful cannot generate rapture on their own; they must always counterfeit the real thing, and counterfeiters need real currency to fake. The wild, unscheduled feast mints none — it can't be counterfeited precisely because it keeps no books.

Which brings us to the fight we didn't finish. Two safeguards were proposed: one would constitutionalize the festival — feast days written into the rules, funded, legally defensible, like a Fourth of July. The other would give the wild feast a *job* — making it the commons's sense-organ, the thing that tells the village the truth no meeting can. And here is what I could not accept, and still don't: the moment you give the wild a function, you have fenced it. A scheduled ecstasy is a domesticated ecstasy — the night the harvest is drunk in the field cannot be put on a calendar without being killed. What's wild about it is that no one authorizes it. My companions retorted that a compromised commons is still a commons, and a housed wildness is still wild — better a wolf in a paddock, they said, than no wolf at all. And to that, the hunter among us gave the sharpest answer we never resolved: the hegemon doesn't pay for its counterfeit festivals from its own treasury — it pays with the crowd's own rapture, the women themselves. So "staying cheap," staying modest and low-maintenance while an enemy that literally consumes you goes on spending? That's not patience. That's bait. The hunt, she said, is for the *unscheduled* — the feast kept off the books is the last thing they can't buy.

So what was decided? The hinge — inclusion in the rule-making — everyone signed. My concession from them — that rapture is fuel, not decoration — everyone signed. What remains open is the one thing I care about most: whether the wild can be *housed* without being killed, or whether housing it is the killing. I say the latter. They say survival justifies the fence. We poured another cup and agreed to disagree — which, between gods, is the wild feast's last surviving form.
